title: Reading one you have never seen

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a load you called wrong, ringed in red and traced to the source or path you skipped, when you change one part and play it.
interactive.title: What if one part changes?
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Fifteen small screens follow. Some show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. The main picture shows one sheet at a time, from a picker of five. Four are new: a compressed air system, a second switchboard, a hoist's control schematic and a drawing of an angle bracket. The fifth is the first switchboard, with sections A and B. Along the top sit four tabs: Legend, Sources, State and Trace. Legend lights the key and the notes. Sources rings every place supply can come in. State lights the notes on how it is drawn. Trace lights one path at a time. Tap a load, and its path back to a source lights. A What if button sits beside the tabs. With it on, tap a part to change it. A valve shuts, a breaker trips, a contact opens, or a compressor or generator stops. Mark each load Stops or Runs, then tap Play. The sheet plays the change slowly. Every load you marked wrong is ringed in red. On a puzzle screen, your choice takes the place of the marks. After Check, the sheet plays it and rings in red what the answer missed. Sheet 1, the compressed air system. Compressors C1 and C2 sit at the bottom left. Each is a circle with a hollow triangle at its outlet, driven by its own motor. After each comes a non-return valve, NR1 and NR2. Its arrow shows the one way it passes. Then comes a hand valve, V1 and V2. The two lines join and run up into the air receiver R1, on the right. It is a tall tank with rounded ends. R1's gauge has no numbers, only a working mark and a low mark. Drain valve V8, marked N.C., sits at R1's foot. From R1, V3 leads to the header, a line across the top. Off the header, V4 feeds the tools, V5 the valve actuators and V6 the hose point. A bypass with V7, marked N.C., runs from the joined compressor line straight to the header, round R1 and V3. The legend says every valve is drawn alike. N.C. means normally closed, shut as drawn. Note 1 says V7 is opened only while V3 is out of service. The rule. A user has air while an open path joins it to a running compressor. So does an open path to R1, while R1's needle is above its low mark. Air passes a non-return valve only its arrow's way. A line carrying air is bold, with arrows. An empty one is pale. With both compressors stopped, R1's needle falls while any user is open. Sheet 2, the second switchboard, drawn with its supplies at the bottom. A feeder from the main board comes in through incoming breaker -Q6 to section 1, on the left. Generator -G4 comes in through its breaker -Q7 to section 2, on the right. Bus-tie -Q8 joins the two sections. Above, section 1 feeds fan -M5 through -Q31 and lighting -E5 through -Q32. Section 2 feeds pump -M6 through -Q41 and heater -E6 through -Q42. The caption says it is drawn as run. -G4 is stopped, -Q7 open and everything else closed. Each load's lamp is lit when it has supply. The rule. A line is live when an unbroken path of closed breakers joins it to a live source. The feeder is always live. -G4 stays stopped. In What if, a tap on it says why. Sheet 3, the hoist's control schematic, drawn the IEC way. A small picture of the hoist and its hook sits beside it. Supply L runs along the top, and return N along the bottom. Stop button -S10 and overload contact -F11, both normally closed, sit on the shared line at the top. Below them stand three current paths. Path 1: Up button -S11, normally open, top limit switch -B11, normally closed, a normally closed contact of -K12, then the coil of Up contactor -K11. Path 2: Down button -S12, bottom limit switch -B12, a normally closed contact of -K11, then the coil of Down contactor -K12. Path 3: normally open contacts of -K11 and -K12 side by side, then brake coil -Y11. With -Y11 energised, the brake lifts. With it dead, the brake's spring holds the hook. Under each coil is its cross-reference. Under -K11, 3 marks its normally open contact and 2 its normally closed one. Under -K12, 3 and then 1. The motor and main contacts are on the power sheet, not drawn. With no latching contacts, the hoist moves only while a button is held. Each contact is drawn faint at rest, with its present state in bold over it. In What if, tapping -B11 or -B12 opens it, as the hook would at the end of its travel. The rule. A coil pulls in while an unbroken path of closed contacts joins it from L to N. Each contact follows the coil whose tag it carries. The hook rises while -K11 is in and falls while -K12 is in. Otherwise the brake holds it. Sheet 4, a first-angle drawing of an angle bracket. It has a flat base, and an upright along its back edge with a hole through it. The front view is in the middle. The view from above is below it, and the view from the left end is on its right. Only two sizes are written, in millimetres. The overall height, 60, runs from the base's underside to the top of the upright. The base is 10 thick. The title block gives the drawing number, issue B, the scale 1 : 2 and the first-angle symbol. Here Legend lights the title block and the symbol. Sources lights the front view, where you start. State lights the issue letter, and Trace the hole through the upright in each view in turn. Sheet 5, the first switchboard, as before. -G1 is on section A, and -G2 and the shore supply on section B. Bus-tie -Q4, N.O., sits between them. Pump -M3 is fed from section A through -Q13, and from section B through -Q23, N.O. An interlock, a dashed link, lets only one of them close at a time. Battery -G3 joins only the DC board, through -Q5. Screen 1, do, What still runs?: the air sheet, both compressors running, every user lit. "Both compressors stop. Do the tools still get air?" Choices: Yes, for a while, from the receiver (right); No, they stop at once; Yes, for as long as you like. Why: R1 is a tank of air under pressure. With both compressors stopped, it still feeds the header. Its pressure falls as the users take air. Then the users stop. So R1 counts as a source until it runs down. After Check, the compressors stop. The users stay lit until R1's needle reaches the low mark. Screen 2, show, Four steps: the air sheet, at rest. Words: "Read a sheet you have never seen in four steps. Find the legend, then every source. Then find the state it is drawn in. Last, trace one path at a time." Then "Tap each tab in turn." Read: Legend lights the key. Sources rings C1, C2 and R1. State lights Note 1 and the N.C. marks. Trace lights the path from C1 through R1 and V3 to the tools. Still: Trace on. Screen 3, do, Read its legend: the air sheet, V7 picked out, the legend dim. "Every valve on this sheet is drawn hollow. Is V7 open or shut as drawn?" Choices: Shut (right); Open; The sheet cannot tell you. Hint on Open: "On some sheets, hollow means open. Read this sheet's legend." Hint on cannot tell: "Look at the mark beside V7. Then find it in the legend." Why: this legend draws every valve alike. N.C. beside a valve means normally closed, shut as drawn. V7 carries N.C. Another sheet may fill in a shut valve instead. So read each sheet's own legend. Screen 4, show, Sources first: the second switchboard. Words: "This board's supplies come in at the bottom. Its loads sit at the top. Read it from the top left, and you start at a load. So find the sources first, wherever they are drawn." Then "Tap Sources. Then turn on What if, change one part, and mark each load before you play it." Read: two sources are ringed, the feeder from the main board through -Q6, and generator -G4 through -Q7. With What if on, you change one part and mark each load Runs or Stops. Play then rings in red any mark that was wrong. Still: Sources on. Screen 5, do, typed, Count the sources: the second switchboard, Sources off. "How many sources can feed this board?" A typed answer: 2, a whole number. Slips: 1, "The cable from the main board counts. To this board, it is where power comes in."; 3, "Bus-tie -Q8 joins the two sections. It carries power across, but it makes none." Hint: "A source is anywhere power can come in. Look along the bottom of the sheet." Why: power can come in two ways, the feeder through -Q6 and generator -G4 through -Q7. Each counts as a source, whether or not it is running now. Screen 6, show, The state it is drawn in: the second switchboard, its caption lit. Words: "Each part is drawn in one state, usually at rest or in its normal position. A caption may say how the plant is run. Here -G4 is stopped, so section 2 is fed from section 1 through bus-tie -Q8." Then "Tap State." Read: the caption is lit. Section 2 is bold through -Q8, and -G4's line is pale. Still: State on. Screen 7, do, What if -Q8 trips?: the second switchboard as run. "Bus-tie -Q8 trips open. What stops?" Choices: Pump -M6 and heater -E6 (right); Nothing, because -G4 feeds section 2; All four loads. Hint on Nothing: "Read the caption. Is -G4 running?" Hint on All four: "Trace fan -M5 back to a source. Does its path pass -Q8?" Why: -G4 is stopped and -Q7 is open. So section 2 has no live source of its own. Its only path to the feeder ran through -Q8. Section 1 still joins the feeder through -Q6. So fan -M5 and lighting -E5 still run. After Check, section 2 goes pale. Screen 8, show, One path at a time: the hoist sheet, the hook mid-travel. Words: "On a control sheet, trace one path at a time, from the supply line to a coil. Then find each contact by its tag, wherever it is drawn. One part can act on several paths." Then "Hold Up." Read: path 1 is bold from L through -S10, -F11, -S11, -B11 and -K12's contact to coil -K11. -K11's contact in path 2 opens. Its contact in path 3 closes. So -Y11 lifts the brake, and the hook rises. Still: Up held. Screen 9, do, What if the top limit opens?: the hoist, the hook at the top, -B11 open. "The hook has reached the top, so -B11 is open. You hold Up, then Down. What happens?" Choices: Up does nothing, and Down still works (right); Neither button works; Up still works. Hint on Neither: "Trace path 2 to coil -K12. Does -B11 sit on it?" Hint on Up still works: "-B11 sits in path 1, the path to coil -K11." Why: -B11 sits only in path 1. Once open, it breaks the path to -K11. So Up does nothing. Path 2 does not pass it, so -K12 still pulls in. -K12's contact in path 3 feeds -Y11. So the brake lifts for the way down. Screen 10, show, The odd one out: the bracket drawing. Words: "An engineering drawing has no sources, and nothing flows through it. So read its title block and issue first, then its projection symbol. Then follow one feature at a time across the views." Then "Tap Trace." Read: the title block gives issue B, the scale 1 : 2 and the first-angle symbol. The hole through the upright lights in each view in turn: a circle in the front view, dashed lines in the other two. Still: Trace on. Screen 11, do, typed, Read the sizes: the bracket drawing, its two sizes lit. "The overall height is 60, and the base is 10 thick. How high does the upright stand above the base's top face?" A typed answer: 50, in mm, a whole number. Slips: 60, "That is the overall height, from the base's underside to the top."; 70, "That adds the base on. The overall height already includes it." Hint: "Does the overall height include the base?" Why: the overall height includes the base. So the upright stands 60 − 10 = 50 mm above the base's top face. Screen 12, do, mixed, Isolate the receiver: the air sheet as drawn. "You must open receiver R1 for an inspection. Which valves do you shut?" Choices: V1, V2 and V3, with V7 kept shut (right); V3 only; V1 and V2 only. Why: air comes into R1 from the compressors, through V1 and V2, and leaves for the header through V3. Shut all three, and every path to R1 stops at a shut valve. V7 would join R1's inlet line to the header. So check it stays shut. R1 still holds air under pressure. Vent it through V8 before you open it. Screen 13, do, mixed, Every way in: the first switchboard as drawn. "You must work on pump -M3's starter, so you lock off -Q13. What else must you lock off before you start?" Choices: -Q23, from section B (right); Bus-tie -Q4, between the sections; Battery -G3, on the DC board. Why: -M3 is fed from section A through -Q13, and from section B through -Q23. -Q23 is open as drawn, but once -Q13 is open, the interlock lets someone at the board close it. So lock off both, then prove it dead at the starter. After Check, -Q13 is locked off, and -Q23 too if right. If wrong, -Q23 and its path to -M3 are ringed in red. Screen 14, do, mixed, Report it: the hoist sheet at rest. "A colleague has never seen this sheet. Which report gives them its key features?" Choices: Each direction needs its limit switch closed and the other contactor out. Either contactor lifts the brake. (right); Each button drives the hook its own way. The limit switches stop it at each end.; Each button feeds its own coil. The brake holds the hook while it moves. Why: Up needs -B11 closed and -K12 out. Down needs -B12 closed and -K11 out. Either one lifts the brake through path 3. After Check, Up is held, then Down. Screen 15, do, mixed, Sheet and plant: the air sheet beside a sketch of the plant as fitted. In the plant, R1 stands left of the compressors, and an untagged pipe runs from R1 straight to the hose point, round V3. "You plan to cut off the header and its users by shutting V3. Compare the plant with the sheet. Is V3 enough?" Choices: No, the plant has a way round V3 (right); No, because R1 sits somewhere else; Yes, V3 is enough. Why: where a part sits does not change what it is joined to. The untagged pipe is a way in the sheet does not show. With V3 shut, R1 still feeds the hose point, and back through V6 the whole header. After Check, V3 shuts on both. The sheet's users lose air. The plant's keep it, and the pipe and all three users are ringed.
interactive.ignores: These sheets are made up for practice. Real ones carry far more parts. They often run across several sheets, joined by cross-references. Every line is simply live or dead, with no pressures, voltages or flows. R1's needle falls far faster than a real receiver's would, so you can watch it. A shut valve and an open breaker cut off perfectly here. A non-return valve never lets any by. Real ones can let a little through. That is why you still prove dead, or vent, at the point of work. Breakers trip only when you tap them. Protection settings are not shown, nor how a fault chooses which breaker trips. The plant sketch is a drawing, not a photograph. Nothing here shows how any real ship's or submarine's systems are laid out or drawn.

explain.text:
You can read a sheet you have never seen in four steps. Find the legend, then every source, then the state it is drawn in. Then trace one path at a time. After that, you can ask what one change does. What stops, and what still runs?

Start with the legend and the notes, because conventions change from sheet to sheet. One sheet fills in a shut valve. Another draws every valve alike. It marks the shut ones N.C., for normally closed. The notes and legend can also say what a symbol alone cannot.[^1]

Next, find every source, wherever it is drawn. A single-line diagram usually starts at the top, with the incoming supply.[^2] A sheet you have never seen may not. If you read it from the top left, you may start at a load. Then you may never see a second way in. A source is anywhere supply can come in. On a board, that is a generator, a feeder from another board or a battery. On a piping or air sheet, it is a pump or a compressor. A store counts too. An [[air receiver]] is a tank of compressed air. It still feeds the line after both compressors stop, until its pressure falls.

Then find the state it is drawn in. Each symbol shows its part in one state, normal or at rest, unless the sheet says otherwise.[^3] A caption may also say how the plant is run. It may say which generator is stopped, for example. A generator drawn on the sheet feeds nothing while it is stopped. A line drawn joined to it is live only if another path joins it to a running source.

Last, trace one path at a time, from a source to a load. On a control sheet, trace from the supply line to a coil. Then find each contact by its tag. One part can act on several paths. Each path needs its own trace. On the hoist, the hook opens a switch near the top when it gets there. It is the top [[limit switch]], -B11. It sits only in the path to the Up contactor, -K11. So when it opens, Up stops, but Down still works.

An engineering drawing is the odd one out. It has no sources, and nothing flows through it. So read its title block and issue first, then its projection symbol. Then follow one feature at a time across the views.

Whatever the sheet, check it against the plant before you rely on it. Every isolation point on the plant should match the drawing.[^4] A pipe fitted after the sheet was drawn is a way in that the sheet does not show. A starter that stays live after you lock off its breaker has another way in too. The sources step finds that way in before you start work.

**Read any sheet in four steps: legend, sources, state, then one path at a time. Then check it against the plant.**

analogy.text: You know this from a periodic inspection of an installation you have never seen. You read the circuit chart and the labels first. You find the origin, and any second source, such as solar panels or a battery. You note how things are set before you touch them. Then you test one circuit at a time. You read a new sheet the same way: key, sources, state, then one path at a time.
analogy.breaks: On site you test the real installation. Your tester tells you what is live. A sheet tells you only what should be there. It cannot show a change made after it was drawn. So you still check the plant itself.

practice.text:
**Safety first:** a sheet tells you what should be there, not what is. Before you isolate, check each isolation point on the plant against it. Then prove dead, or vent, at the point of work.

- Read the title block. Check that the drawing number and its issue are the current ones.
- Read the legend and the notes. Do not carry symbols over from another sheet.
- Find every source, wherever it is drawn. Sources include generators, feeders from other boards, batteries, pumps, compressors, and stores such as an air receiver.
- Find the state it is drawn in. Read every note or caption on how the plant is run.
- Trace one path at a time, from a source to a load. On a control sheet, trace from the supply line to a coil. Then follow each contact by its tag.
- Change one thing at a time. Then ask, for every load, whether it stops or still runs. Check them all, not just the one you expect.
- On an engineering drawing, read the title block and the projection symbol. Then follow one feature across the views.

**Rule of thumb:** start at the sources, not at the top left. Count the ways in before you count the ways out.

**Worked example:** the second switchboard, with bus-tie -Q8 tripped. Legend: plain breaker symbols, with a caption for the state. Sources: two, the feeder through -Q6 and generator -G4 through -Q7. State: -G4 is stopped and -Q7 is open. So the feeder carries both sections, through -Q8. Trace: section 1 still joins the feeder through -Q6. So fan -M5 and lighting -E5 still run. Section 2 joined it only through -Q8. So pump -M6 and heater -E6 stop.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading from the top left, and starting at a load.
- Missing a source that is a store, such as a battery or an air receiver.
- Missing a feeder from another board, because it does not look like a generator.
- Taking a breaker drawn open as one that is locked off.
- Reading one sheet with another sheet's legend.
- Taking a source drawn on the sheet as live, without reading how the plant is run.
- Tracing one path and stopping, when a part acts on several.
- Trusting the sheet without checking it against the plant.
